lead: You'll write the brief for a small product that joins two sources of work information, and Cowork will turn it into a one-page plan you build from for the rest of this level. This level expects you to fill in the brief yourself: the bracketed parts are decisions only you can make.
why: A plan with a clear acceptance test keeps a build with many parts on track, and the later missions in this level read from it.
result: A one-page product plan, product-plan.md, with a testable definition of done, saved in your Cowork Academy folder.

think.scene: At work: the biggest wins connect two systems that don't talk to each other today.
think.ask: Which two systems do people at your company bridge by hand?

steps.goal: State the problem, the users and a test for success, so Cowork can question your idea before anything gets planned or built.
steps.title: Write your product brief
steps.do: Replace every bracketed part with your own decision. Then paste it into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: I'm planning a small internal product for my team at a vacation rental company. Problem: [the problem in one sentence]. Users: [who uses it, and when]. Sources: [two sources, e.g. maintenance-tickets.csv and guest-reviews.csv]. Done means: [a test you could check, e.g. a manager sees which homes need attention in under a minute]. Ask me up to 4 questions about anything unclear, one at a time.
steps.see: Cowork asks you a single question, such as how often the users would open the product or what they do today instead. Notice that it asks before writing anything.
steps.stuck: No idea yet? Use the example: a property health hub that combines maintenance-tickets.csv and guest-reviews.csv, both already in your Cowork Academy folder. If Cowork writes a plan straight away, reply: 'Stop. Ask me your questions first, one at a time.'

steps.goal: Answer Cowork's questions so it can turn your brief into a one-page plan, product-plan.md, that every later mission builds from.
steps.title: Answer questions and save the plan
steps.do: Answer each question in a sentence or two. After the last one, fill in the brackets below, paste it into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Write a one-page plan and save it in this folder as product-plan.md. Sections: problem and users, the done test, data sources, the pages of a small internal website, one job I'd delegate: [e.g. a weekly review of low-rated stays], one task to save as a skill: [e.g. replying to a guest complaint in our voice], and open questions.
steps.see: product-plan.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with a short section for each item. Notice that your done test appears word for word.
steps.stuck: If a section is vague, such as 'a messaging app', reply: 'Name the exact source for each section and update product-plan.md.'

steps.goal: Have Cowork attack the plan the way a skeptical decision-maker would, so weak spots get cut now, before you spend time building.
steps.title: Pressure-test the plan
steps.do: Fill in the bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Read product-plan.md as a skeptical [who will judge it, e.g. our operations manager]. Does every section serve the done test? List up to 3 gaps, and suggest one thing to cut. Update the file only after I agree.
steps.see: Up to three specific gaps and one suggested cut. Notice whether each gap ties back to your done test. After you agree, Cowork updates product-plan.md.
steps.stuck: If Cowork says the plan is fine, ask: 'Which section would fail first if we built it tomorrow?'

steps.q: You draft your brief and the done test says: 'The site looks good and the team likes it.' What should you change before you build?
options: Leave it open, so the plan can change as you build
Make it something you can check, like a time
Add more pages, so there's more for the team to like
steps.why: A done test you can check tells you, and Cowork, when the work is finished. Leaving it open feels flexible, but then nobody can say whether the product works.

lead: You'll have Cowork build a small internal website from your plan, then review it from your users' point of view. At this level you write the brief: you decide the pages and what the site must let people do.
why: A clear, accessible internal page gets used. A confusing one gets ignored.
result: A multi-page internal website in a site folder, reviewed for design, wording and accessibility against your own done test.

think.scene: At work: an internal portal that's clear and accessible gets used, and an ugly one gets ignored.
think.ask: What internal page would people actually bookmark?

steps.goal: Turn product-plan.md into a working set of linked pages, so you have something real to test in place of a description.
steps.title: Build the website from your plan
steps.do: Fill in the brackets, then paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Read product-plan.md (or sample-business-brief.md if you don't have one). Build the internal website it describes as linked HTML pages in a new folder called site: [the pages, e.g. a home page, a property list and an open issues page]. It must [your done test, e.g. let a manager find any property's open issues in two clicks] and work at phone width. Use sample data from the practice files.
steps.see: A folder called site appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with index.html and the other pages you asked for. Notice whether the pages match the ones in your plan.
steps.stuck: Don't have product-plan.md? The prompt falls back to sample-business-brief.md, which is already in your folder. If neither is there, describe your product in two sentences at the start of the prompt.

steps.goal: Use the site as one of your users would, so you find out whether it passes your done test before asking Cowork to polish it.
steps.title: Click through the site yourself
steps.do: Open index.html from the site folder in your Cowork Academy folder. Click every link, then try your done test as if you were one of your users.
steps.see: The site opens in your web browser, every link works, and you can tell whether your done test passes. Note anything confusing to feed into the next step.
steps.stuck: If it opens as code in a text editor, right-click index.html and choose to open it with your web browser.

steps.goal: Have Cowork review the site from your user's point of view for design, wording and accessibility, then fix what it finds, so the finished site works for real people.
steps.title: Review the site and fix it
steps.do: Fill in the brackets, then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Review the site as [your user, e.g. a housekeeper checking it on a phone between cleans]. Do a design critique, a plain-language pass and an accessibility check (contrast, text size, tap targets). List the top 3 issues in each, fix them, and confirm the site still passes: [your done test]. Also fix this, which I found: [one thing that bothered you].
steps.see: Three short lists of issues, a summary of what Cowork changed, and a line on whether the done test still passes. Refresh the page in your browser to see the fixes.
steps.stuck: If the fixes don't show, refresh the browser page. If the site still feels like a first draft, ask: 'Do a second, tighter design pass, and show me what you changed.'

steps.q: The first draft looks fine on your laptop. Your users are housekeepers who check it on their phones between cleans. What do you do next?
options: Review it at phone width as they would, then fix
Send them the link and gather feedback next week
Ask for a few new designs and pick the best one
steps.why: A review from the user's point of view catches problems you won't see on a laptop, like tiny tap targets. Sending it out first means your users find the problems for you.

t: Delegate a job and build a skill
lead: You'll write a delegation brief for a self-contained job, judge what comes back, then save a repeatable task as a custom skill. This level expects you to fill in the brief: the goal, scope, sources and output format are yours to decide.
why: A clear brief is how you hand off a big job, whoever or whatever does it, and a skill lets you repeat a task the same way every time.
result: agent-result.md from your own delegation brief, and a saved custom skill tested in a new task.

think.scene: At work: an agent researches every new lead, and a skill drafts the first outreach in the company's style.
think.ask: Which multi-step process could split into a "research" part and a "draft" part?

steps.goal: Hand Cowork a self-contained job with a clear goal, scope, sources and output format, so it can work alone and you can judge the result against something specific.
steps.title: Write a delegation brief
steps.do: Fill in all four parts of the brief: goal, scope, sources and output format. Then paste it into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt:
Treat this as a delegated job and follow the brief exactly.
Goal: [the decision this helps, e.g. which property a manager should visit first].
Scope: [what's in and out, e.g. reviews from June to September 2026, no guest contact].
Sources: guest-reviews.csv and [any other file, or none].
Output format: [e.g. a ranked table of the 3 weakest properties with the reviews behind each].
Save the result as agent-result.md.
steps.see: Cowork works through the job, then agent-result.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder. Notice whether it follows the format you asked for.
steps.stuck: Cowork may do the job in this task or hand it to a helper, depending on your setup. Either is fine: you're practicing the brief. If the result misses, change the brief part that caused it and run it again.

steps.goal: Hold the result up to your four brief parts and ask for the working behind key numbers, so you trust delegated work only after checking it.
steps.title: Check the result against your brief
steps.do: Open agent-result.md and compare it with your four brief parts. Then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Check agent-result.md against my brief, part by part: goal, scope, sources and output format. Say where it falls short, and show me how you got the two most important numbers so I can check them in guest-reviews.csv.
steps.see: A part-by-part check against your brief, and the working behind two numbers, such as a property's average rating and how many reviews it's based on. Notice any part that fell short.
steps.stuck: If the working doesn't match the file, ask: 'Recalculate that from guest-reviews.csv and show me the rows you used.'

steps.goal: Save a task you do again and again as a custom skill with your own quality criteria, so you never have to re-explain it.
steps.title: Turn a repeated task into a skill
steps.do: Fill in the brackets, then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Create a custom skill for a task I repeat: [the task, e.g. replying to a guest complaint in our voice]. Good output means: [your criteria, e.g. under 120 words, apologizes once, offers one concrete fix, promises no refunds]. Ask me for one real-looking example before you write it.
steps.see: Cowork asks for an example, then creates the skill. It may ask you to approve the skill or turn it on. Notice that your criteria are written into it.
steps.stuck: If Cowork asks you to approve or turn on the skill, do it. If you can't find where, check Claude's help center at support.claude.com, or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.goal: Run the skill in a fresh task to prove it works without any of the earlier context, which is how you'll use it from now on.
steps.title: Test the skill in a new task
steps.do: Start a new Cowork task in your Cowork Academy folder. Fill in the bracket, then paste this and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Use my [skill name] skill on the lowest-rated review in agent-result.md (or in guest-reviews.csv if you don't have that file). Save the output as skill-test.md, and tell me which of the skill's criteria it met.
steps.see: skill-test.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder, written to your criteria, with a note on which ones it met. Notice whether any criterion was missed.
steps.stuck: If Cowork doesn't seem to know the skill, check that you approved it or turned it on, then name the skill again in your request.

steps.q: Your brief asked for the 3 weakest properties, but agent-result.md ranks all 12 in a long essay. What should you change?
options: The goal, so it asks for a full portfolio review
The output format, with a set count and layout
Nothing, since more detail gives you more to use
steps.why: Length and layout come from the output format part of the brief, so that's the part to tighten. Changing the goal would make the result fit by asking for something you don't need.

lead: You'll have Cowork read two sources of work information and match them up into drafts, for example guest messages checked against open repair tickets. This level expects you to fill in the brief: you decide what starts the workflow, what gets matched and what the drafts say.
why: A lot of manual work is moving information from one place to another. With both sources in reach, Cowork can do the bridging and you approve the result.
result: bridge-drafts.md: drafts that combine information from two sources, with nothing sent, changed or deleted.

think.scene: At work: new rows in a spreadsheet become calendar holds and draft emails automatically.
think.ask: Where does information arrive in one place and then need to go somewhere else?

steps.goal: Confirm Cowork can read both of your sources before you build on them, so a connection problem shows up now and not halfway through.
steps.title: Test both sources work
steps.do: Only connect apps your company has approved, and sign in yourself in any pop-up. Then fill in the brackets, paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Show me one small sample from each of these two sources so I know both work: [source 1, e.g. guest-messages.txt or my company calendar] and [source 2, e.g. maintenance-tickets.csv or a shared team sheet]. Don't send, change or delete anything.
steps.see: A short sample from each source, for example two guest messages and the first few rows of the tickets. Notice that you can recognise the data as yours.
steps.stuck: Use a real inbox or calendar only if your company has approved this connector. Otherwise, use guest-messages.txt and maintenance-tickets.csv, which are already in your folder. For help connecting an approved app, check support.claude.com or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.goal: Tell Cowork what starts the workflow, what to take from each source and what each draft should say, so it matches the two sources into drafts.
steps.title: Describe the workflow to build
steps.do: Fill in every bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Build one workflow from these two sources. Starts when: [the trigger, e.g. a guest message mentions a repair]. From source 1, take: [e.g. the property and the problem]. Match it in source 2 with: [e.g. open tickets for that property]. Each draft must: [your criteria, e.g. give the guest a realistic next step and name the ticket]. Save all drafts in this folder as bridge-drafts.md. Don't send, change or delete anything.
steps.see: bridge-drafts.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with one draft per matched item. Notice that each draft names details from both sources.
steps.stuck: If Cowork starts to send or change something, reply: 'Stop. Drafts in bridge-drafts.md only.' Then check the app to see whether anything changed.

steps.goal: Check two drafts against the original items yourself, because a match that looks right can still pair the wrong records.
steps.title: Verify two drafts by hand
steps.do: Open bridge-drafts.md. Pick two drafts and check each one against the original item in both sources.
steps.see: Each draft you checked names the right item from source 1 and the right match from source 2. Nothing has been sent, changed or deleted.
steps.stuck: If a draft matched the wrong item, tell Cowork which one and why, and ask it to tighten the matching rule and redo bridge-drafts.md.

steps.q: Your workflow matches guest messages to repair tickets and saves drafts. One draft tells a guest their AC is fixed, but the ticket is still Open. What do you do?
options: Close the ticket so the two sources agree again
Send it anyway, since the guest will flag any issue
Fix the draft, then tighten the matching rule
steps.why: The draft is wrong, and the rule that made it will repeat the mistake, so fix both. Closing the ticket makes the sources agree but leaves the guest with a broken AC.

lead: You'll build a dashboard from the bookings and maintenance data, with 4 or 5 signals and a 'what changed' summary, and learn to refresh it by rebuilding. This level expects you to fill in the brief: you decide who reads it and what decision each signal supports.
why: A dashboard you can rebuild in one paste can replace a meeting that exists only to share numbers.
result: dashboard.html with 4 or 5 decision-led signals, plus refresh.md, a saved prompt that rebuilds it from the newest data.

think.scene: At work: a weekly "what changed and why" summary replaces a status meeting.
think.ask: Which meeting exists only to share numbers?

steps.goal: Decide which 4 or 5 numbers the dashboard shows and what decision each one supports, so every tile earns its place.
steps.title: Choose the signals to track
steps.do: bookings.csv and maintenance-tickets.csv are already in your Cowork Academy folder. Fill in the brackets, then paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Read product-plan.md (or sample-business-brief.md if you don't have one). Using bookings.csv and maintenance-tickets.csv, propose 4 or 5 signals for a dashboard read by [who, e.g. the Monday operations meeting]. Each signal must help decide [the decision, e.g. which property or channel needs action this week]. Drop any signal that doesn't lead to a decision.
steps.see: A short list of signals, each with the decision it supports, such as 'Open HVAC tickets by property: who to send a vendor to.' Notice that every signal leads to an action.
steps.stuck: If a signal has no clear decision, reply: 'Replace that one with a signal someone would act on this week.'

steps.goal: Turn the agreed signals into dashboard.html with a 'what changed' summary on top, plus refresh.md so you can rebuild it later.
steps.title: Build the dashboard
steps.do: Fill in the bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter. Open dashboard.html from your folder when it's ready.
steps.prompt: Build those signals as dashboard.html in this folder, one tile each, with a 'what changed' summary at the top comparing September 2026 with August 2026. It must pass this test: [your done test, e.g. a manager can name the top problem in 30 seconds]. Also save refresh.md with the exact prompt I can paste to rebuild it from the newest data.
steps.see: dashboard.html opens in your browser with a tile per signal and a short summary at the top. Notice what the summary says changed. refresh.md is in your folder.
steps.stuck: If dashboard.html opens as code, right-click it and choose to open it with your web browser. The file doesn't update by itself: you refresh it by asking Cowork to rebuild it.

steps.goal: Add one new ticket to a copy of the data and rebuild, to show the dashboard really updates when the data changes.
steps.title: Prove the refresh works
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter. Coming back later with newer data to use refresh.md is optional.
steps.prompt: Copy maintenance-tickets.csv to tickets-test.csv and add one Open HVAC ticket at Summit Lodge, dated 2026-09-30, costing $900. Rebuild the dashboard from tickets-test.csv as dashboard-test.html, and tell me which tiles changed.
steps.see: dashboard-test.html appears in your folder, and Cowork names the tiles that changed, such as Summit Lodge's maintenance cost or the count of open tickets. Notice that only the affected tiles moved.
steps.stuck: If Cowork edits maintenance-tickets.csv itself, ask it to undo that change. Other missions rely on the original file.

steps.q: Your 'what changed' summary compares September 2026 with August 2026 in bookings.csv. What does it show for revenue?
options: It held at about $82,750
It rose to about $85,680
It fell to about $53,500
steps.why: Revenue fell from $82,754 in August to $53,501 in September. $85,684 was July, the strongest month, so a summary claiming a rise has mixed up the months.

t: Automate the web with Claude in Chrome
lead: You'll have Cowork use your web browser to collect information for your product from a site with no export button. This level expects you to fill in the brief: you decide the site, what to collect and how you'll know it's right.
why: Optional: this needs the Claude in Chrome browser extension, which may not be available to you. When it works, it ends copying information out of websites by hand.
result: web-results.md, collected by Cowork in your browser and spot-checked by you.

think.scene: At work: nobody copies data out of a vendor portal that has no export button anymore.
think.ask: Which website do you copy information from by hand?

steps.goal: Check that Cowork can use your browser before you plan a task around it, so you don't brief a job it can't do.
steps.title: Confirm Chrome access
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Can you use my Chrome browser through Claude in Chrome in this task right now? Answer yes or no, and don't change any settings.
steps.see: A clear yes or no. If no, stop and check that Claude in Chrome is installed and turned on before moving on.
steps.stuck: If the answer is no, or your company doesn't allow browser extensions, skip this mission. Nothing later in this level depends on it. For setup help, check support.claude.com or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.goal: Have Cowork visit a site with no export button and collect what you need into a file, saving you from copying it by hand.
steps.title: Send Cowork to collect from a site
steps.do: Fill in every bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter. If the site asks you to sign in, do it yourself.
steps.prompt: Using Claude in Chrome, go to [a site you use for work, e.g. a supplier's price list]. Collect [what you need, e.g. prices for our 5 most-ordered cleaning supplies]. Done means: [your test, e.g. every item has a price, a unit size and the page it came from]. Don't buy, submit or send anything. Save it in this folder as web-results.md.
steps.see: Chrome moves through the site while Cowork reports what it's doing. Then web-results.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder. Notice that it lists only what you asked for.
steps.stuck: If Cowork asks to submit, buy or send something, say no. If the site blocks it, try a public page with the same kind of information.

steps.goal: Compare two collected items with the live site yourself, since web collection can misread a page without any warning.
steps.title: Spot-check against the website
steps.do: Pick two items in web-results.md and compare them with the website yourself.
steps.see: Both items match what the site shows today, and each one meets your done test.
steps.stuck: If something doesn't match, reply: 'The entry for [item] doesn't match the site. Check it again and show me where you found it.'

steps.q: Cowork has collected supplier prices and reaches a reorder form with a Submit button. What should happen next?
options: Cowork stops, and you decide on submitting
Cowork submits, since the prices were checked
Cowork submits a small test order to try it
steps.why: Anything that submits, sends or spends stays with you. Checked prices don't make an order safe to place: the quantities and delivery details still need your eyes.

lead: You'll have Cowork control a desktop app on your computer, clicking and typing, to do one small, reversible task. This level expects you to fill in the brief: you pick the task and the test for whether it worked.
why: Optional: computer control depends on your setup and may not be available to you. When it works, it handles tasks in apps that have no connector.
result: One small, reversible task done by Cowork in a desktop app, checked by you.

think.scene: At work: Cowork renames, sorts and files hundreds of documents in minutes.
think.ask: What file or folder cleanup keeps getting put off?

steps.goal: Check that Cowork can control apps on your computer before you plan a task around it, and learn what kinds of apps it can use.
steps.title: Confirm desktop control works
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Can you control desktop apps on my computer in this task right now? Answer yes or no, and if yes, name the kinds of apps.
steps.see: A clear yes or no, and if yes, the kinds of apps it can use. Notice which kinds, so you pick a task it can really do.
steps.stuck: If the answer is no, or your company has computer control turned off, skip this mission. Nothing later in this level depends on it. For setup help, check support.claude.com or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.goal: Hand Cowork one small, reversible job in a desktop app, so you can watch it click and type with little risk.
steps.title: Give Cowork one small task
steps.do: Fill in the brackets, then paste this into the same task and press Enter. Read any permission request before you allow it.
steps.prompt: Do one small, reversible task in a desktop app: [the task, e.g. open a text editor and draft a launch checklist from product-plan.md]. Done means: [your test, e.g. a saved file with 8 to 10 checklist items]. Don't delete, send or pay for anything. Tell me exactly what you did.
steps.see: The app opens and you watch Cowork click and type in it, followed by a short report of what it did. Notice whether the report matches what you saw.
steps.stuck: If you're not comfortable with what a permission request allows, deny it and pick a smaller task. Don't have product-plan.md? Use sample-business-brief.md instead.

steps.goal: Look at the app yourself to confirm the work is really there and passes your test, rather than trusting the report alone.
steps.title: Verify the result in the app
steps.do: Open the app yourself and look at what Cowork made or changed.
steps.see: The work is there, matches Cowork's report and passes your done test.
steps.stuck: If anything looks wrong, undo it in the app yourself, then tell Cowork what went wrong.

steps.q: Computer control works for you, and you want to try it on real work. Which task should you start with?
options: Clearing out last year's old booking exports
Sending the weekly owner updates from your email
Drafting a checklist in a new text file
steps.why: Start with something low-stakes and easy to undo. Clearing old files feels harmless, but deleting is hard to reverse, so it stays with you.

lead: You'll see which plugins you can use, check what one adds before installing it, and use it on a task for your product. This level expects you to fill in the brief: you decide the task and what good output looks like.
why: Optional: plugins may not be available in your setup. When they are, a plugin adds a set of skills and connectors at once, so a team gets a ready-made toolkit.
result: One installed plugin and a piece of work made with it that meets your own criteria.

think.scene: At work: a finance or sales plugin gives a team a ready-made toolkit for its specialty.
think.ask: Which department would benefit most from a ready-made toolkit?

steps.goal: Find out which plugins are actually available to you, so you choose from real options and not guesses.
steps.title: See which plugins you can use
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Which plugins can you see that are installed or available to me right now? List only ones you can actually see, with one line on what each adds. If you can't see any, say so.
steps.see: A short list of plugins with what each adds, or a clear statement that none are visible. Notice that it lists only plugins it can actually see.
steps.stuck: If none are available, or your company limits plugins, skip this mission. Nothing later in this level depends on it. To learn where plugins are installed, check support.claude.com or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.goal: Ask what a plugin adds and what it can access, then decide if it fits your product, so you install it knowing the risks.
steps.title: Check a plugin before installing
steps.do: Fill in the bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter. Install it only if what it can access is fine for your work.
steps.prompt: Before I install [a plugin from the list], tell me what it adds and what apps or data it can access. Then tell me whether it fits product-plan.md (or sample-business-brief.md).
steps.see: A short explanation of what the plugin adds and what apps or data it can reach. Once you install it, Cowork may ask you to approve or turn it on.
steps.stuck: If it asks you to sign in to an app, do it yourself, and only for apps your company has approved. If your account can't install plugins, use one that's already installed.

steps.goal: Put the installed plugin to work on a task for your product, and judge the output against your own criteria.
steps.title: Use the plugin on a real task
steps.do: Fill in every bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Use [the plugin] on this task: [the task, e.g. a weekly summary of maintenance-tickets.csv for property owners]. Good output means: [your criteria, e.g. one page, top 3 costs, no internal jargon]. Tell me which skill or tool from the plugin you used, and which criteria the output met.
steps.see: Finished work, plus a note naming the plugin skill or tool Cowork used and how it scored against your criteria. Notice whether it beat your plain Cowork result.
steps.stuck: If Cowork does the work without the plugin, reply: 'Redo this using the plugin, and name the skill you used.'

steps.q: A teammate shares a plugin that adds a reporting skill and an email connector. Before you install it, what should you check first?
options: How many skills it adds, compared with others
What it can access, and if that's approved
Whether the teammate has used it for a while
steps.why: A plugin can bring connectors that reach your apps and data, so check what it can access and whether your company allows that. A teammate's experience helps, but it doesn't tell you what the plugin can reach.

lead: You'll chain a data source, your custom skill and a delegated job into one workflow, test it once, then put it on a schedule. This level expects you to fill in the brief: you design the chain and its done test.
why: This is the difference between using Cowork and building with it: the work runs as a set process, and you review the results.
result: workflow.md, a chain of a source, a skill and a delegated job, with one test run checked by you and a schedule or on-demand plan.

think.scene: At work: a daily process runs by itself overnight, and people review the results in the morning.
think.ask: Which process would you trust to run overnight if you could check the result first?

steps.goal: Link a data source, a delegated job and your custom skill into one written workflow, so a whole process runs from a single plan.
steps.title: Design the workflow chain
steps.do: Fill in every bracket, then paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Read product-plan.md (or sample-business-brief.md). Design one workflow. Input: [a source, e.g. maintenance-tickets.csv or an approved app]. Delegated job: [goal, scope and output format, e.g. rank open tickets by guest impact in a table]. Skill: use my [skill name] skill to [what it does, e.g. draft owner notes for the top 3]. Done means: [your test]. Outbound stays a draft. Save numbered steps as workflow.md.
steps.see: workflow.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with numbered steps. Notice that it names the input, the delegated job, the skill and your done test.
steps.stuck: No custom skill yet? Replace the skill line with two or three written rules, such as 'under 100 words, plain English'. Don't have product-plan.md? The prompt falls back to sample-business-brief.md.

steps.goal: Run the whole chain a single time to see each step hand off to the next, and catch breaks before you automate it.
steps.title: Run the workflow once
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Run workflow.md once now, step by step. Show me what each step produced and where it handed off to the next, then tell me whether the run passed my done test.
steps.see: A run-through of each step and its output, ending with drafts for you to review and a pass or fail against your test. Notice where one step hands off to the next.
steps.stuck: If one step fails, fix it on its own first. Reply: 'Run only step [number] and show me what goes wrong.'

steps.goal: Put the tested workflow on a schedule so it runs without you, with anything outbound kept as drafts for your review.
steps.title: Schedule the workflow
steps.do: Fill in the bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Schedule workflow.md to run [how often, e.g. every Monday at 8am]. Save results in this folder and keep anything outbound as drafts. Tell me the schedule's name and when it runs next.
steps.see: Cowork confirms the schedule's name and the next run time. Note both, so you know when to expect results.
steps.stuck: Scheduled tasks may only run while your computer is on and the Claude app is open. If scheduling isn't available, run it on demand by pasting 'Run workflow.md once now.' To pause or delete a schedule, check support.claude.com or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.q: Monday's scheduled run of workflow.md saved drafts, but the ranking step left out two open tickets. What's the best fix?
options: Run that step alone, fix it, then rerun
Rebuild workflow.md from a fresh brief
Add a check step at the end of the chain
steps.why: Chains break at one link, and testing that link alone shows you what's wrong. A check step at the end might catch it next time, but the broken step would still drop tickets.

lead: You'll tell Cowork what you built, get a 5-minute demo script, then find the weakest part and save a launch summary. This level expects you to fill in the brief: you name the audience and the parts you finished.
why: Being able to explain how each piece works is what makes you the person colleagues come to for help with AI.
result: demo-script.md and launch-summary.md, saved in your Cowork Academy folder.

think.scene: At work: the person who can explain how it all works becomes the company's go-to AI champion.
think.ask: Who would you demo this to, and which of their problems would it solve?

steps.goal: Tell Cowork what you built so it can write a 5-minute demo script, ready for you to present your product to others.
steps.title: Write the demo script
steps.do: Fill in every bracket, then paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Here's what I built: [the parts you finished, e.g. the site folder, dashboard.html, a guest-reply skill, workflow.md]. List the files in this folder to confirm. Then write a 5-minute demo for [your audience, e.g. my operations manager] showing how it meets: [your done test from product-plan.md]. Name the Cowork feature behind each part. Save it as demo-script.md.
steps.see: A list of the files in your folder, then demo-script.md appears, split into timed sections. Notice that each section names the feature behind it.
steps.stuck: Cowork can't see skills or connectors from earlier tasks, so name them yourself in the prompt. If you skipped missions, list only what you finished. Don't have product-plan.md? Write your done test in one sentence instead.

steps.goal: Find the weakest part of your product and the one change that would help most, then record it all in a launch summary.
steps.title: Name the weak spot and summarise
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: What's the single weakest part of this product, and what one change would improve it most? Then save a one-page launch-summary.md: what it does, who it helps, what's built, the weak spot and its fix, and 3 ideas for a next version.
steps.see: One named weak spot with a concrete fix, then launch-summary.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder with what it does, who it helps and what to improve.
steps.stuck: If Cowork lists several weak spots, reply: 'Pick only the one that matters most, and update launch-summary.md.'

steps.q: During your demo, your manager asks why the dashboard's numbers differ from last week's. What shows you really understand the product?
options: Saying that Cowork built it, so you'd ask it
Explaining it's rebuilt from the newest data
Promising to look into it after the meeting
steps.why: Knowing which feature powers each part lets you answer on the spot and fix it later. Deferring to Cowork shows you used it, not that you understand what you built.

lead: You'll check your site folder for anything private, then publish it to a web address you can share. This level expects you to fill in the brief: you decide who it's for and what must stay off it.
why: Optional: skip it if your company doesn't allow public sites or you'd rather keep your work in your folder. Publishing usually takes 30 minutes or more the first time.
result: Your product site, checked for private data and published at a shareable web address.

think.scene: At work: a shared link puts a working tool in front of the people who need it.
think.ask: Who should see what you built, and what would you ask them?

steps.goal: Have Cowork check every file for private details before anything goes public, because published pages are hard to take back.
steps.title: Scan the site for private data
steps.do: Fill in the brackets, then paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Before I publish the site folder for [who will see it, e.g. anyone with the link], check every file. List anything private: guest or owner names, emails, phone numbers, door codes, passwords, internal figures and [anything else that must stay off, e.g. vendor prices]. Suggest a safe replacement for each, and change the files only after I agree.
steps.see: A list of private items with a suggested fix for each, or a clear note that nothing private was found. Notice which files they sit in, and fix them before the next step.
steps.stuck: Don't have a site folder? Skip this mission, or do 'Build the multi-page website' first. If the site includes a dashboard built from real company data, ask: 'Remove the dashboard from the version I publish.'

steps.goal: Put your checked site at a web address you can share, with Cowork guiding one step at a time.
steps.title: Publish the site step by step
steps.do: If your company has an approved place for internal pages, use it and stop here. Otherwise, paste this into the same task, press Enter and follow each step.
steps.prompt: Walk me through publishing the site folder to a free host such as GitHub Pages, one step at a time. Wait for me to finish each step before you give the next one. I'll create any accounts and sign in myself.
steps.see: Only the first step, for example creating a GitHub account, then Cowork waits. At the end you have a web address, and every page loads there on your computer and your phone.
steps.stuck: Check your company's rules about public websites before you publish. A new site can take a few minutes to appear. If a page shows a 404 error, tell Cowork which page and ask it to find the cause.

steps.q: Your site includes a dashboard built from your company's real booking export. You're about to publish to a public address. What do you do?
options: Publish it, since the address is hard to guess
Publish it, but only share the link with your team
Swap in practice data, or leave it off
steps.why: Anyone with the link can see a public page, and links get passed on. Sharing only with your team still leaves real business data one forward away from anyone.
